title: Ephrem, the harp of the Spirit (d. 373)
hookLine: a Syriac deacon who taught theology through women's choirs and hymns

lines: A DEACON AND A CHOIR OF WOMEN.
cards: What does a creed sound like when it's sung? Go east, past the Greek-speaking cities, to churches that pray in Syriac. A deacon there is rehearsing a choir.
The singers are women. The songs are about the birth of Christ, the cross, paradise, the bread of the altar. Arguments about who Christ is are loud in these years, and hard to follow.
This deacon's answer is not a longer argument. It's a rehearsal, verse by verse, until the women know it by heart. His name is Ephrem.

teach.h: A DEACON WHO WROTE IN SONG.
teach.b: Ephrem was a deacon, not a bishop, and he wrote in Syriac, much of it in poems meant to be sung. A later Syriac poet, Jacob of Serugh, wrote a long sung homily in his honor.

teach.h: CHOIRS OF WOMEN TEACH THE CHURCH.
teach.b: Jacob says Ephrem saw that the women of the church were kept silent, so he gathered them into choirs and taught them his hymns, and the women became teachers of the whole assembly.
Doctrine, carried by women's voices, line by line. The letter to the Colossians asks for something like it.
In the Douay-Rheims it speaks of "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles." Ephrem's choirs come close to it. And notice how he does theology.
When people wanted to dissect God, to pin down exactly how the Son is born of the Father, Ephrem pushed back in his hymns on faith.
Some things, he says, are for praising, not for prying into. Across his hymns he turns to pictures instead: the pearl, the womb of Mary, the robe of light Adam lost and Christ gives back.
Scripture and nature, for him, are full of signs pointing to God, and a hymn can hold a sign without flattening it. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit.
The Catholic Church names him a Doctor of the Church, one of the teachers whose writing it holds up for everyone.
For Ephrem, the hymn was the lesson, and the choir was the classroom.

how: The Catholic Church honors Ephrem as a saint and a Doctor of the Church; Syriac Catholic, Maronite and Chaldean Catholics, among others, still pray in liturgies shaped by the Syriac tradition he wrote in.

games.q: you're Ephrem. arguments about who Christ is are everywhere, and ordinary people can't follow them. how do you teach?
o: write a longer argument for the experts.
set the faith to music and teach a choir to sing it.
tell everyone to stop talking about it.
games.why: he wrote hymns and, a later poet says, trained choirs of women to sing them, so the doctrine went out in their voices.

practice: Find a hymn you know, a carol, a verse from Mass, something a grandmother hummed, and sing it quietly, even under your breath. Then listen to the words as if someone were teaching you with them: what do they say about God?
If you don't know a hymn, hum any tune that's been sung in a church and notice what it does to your breathing.

wordCard.voice: Ephrem. A Syriac deacon who taught the faith in hymns and trained choirs of women to sing them. Tradition calls him the harp of the Spirit. Today's word.

orig.note: Syriac: harp of the Spirit — the title tradition gives Ephrem.

carryVoice: Your line: theology you can sing. From Athanasius and the Arian question, through Basil's city of mercy, two Gregorys and Macrina, to a deacon with a choir. That's the week.
